summary: Describes the Multicast Address-Set Claim (MASC) protocol, intended for allocating sets of multicast addresses between domains. It was an experimental protocol and is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: MASC is a protocol for handing out blocks of multicast group addresses to networks. A network that wants addresses picks a block, tells its neighbours, and waits to see whether anyone else wants the same block. If nobody objects, the block belongs to that network, and the network can then share it out to its own users or to the networks below it.

questions: how are multicast addresses allocated between domains
subtitle: How a network claims a block of multicast addresses for its own domain, without two domains claiming the same block.

tldr.problem: Multicast group addresses have to be shared out between networks, and the usual way of doing it did not scale to domains that wanted their own blocks of addresses.
tldr.mechanism: MASC is a claim-collide protocol: a node picks an address prefix, announces the claim, waits while listening for a competing claim, and keeps the prefix only if nobody else claims it. Claims are exchanged over TCP between nodes that play the roles of parent, child, sibling or internal peer.
tldr.outcome: The RFC specifies the full protocol, including the message formats, the constants and the connection state machine. It was an Experimental protocol, the RFC Editor index lists its status as Historic, and no later RFC obsoletes it.

today: RFC 2909 is a September 2000 Experimental protocol, and the RFC Editor index lists its status as Historic. No later RFC obsoletes it, so it is kept here as a record of the Multicast Address-Set Claim protocol.

sections.title: What MASC Does
sections.content:
MASC, the Multicast Address-Set Claim protocol, is a layer 3 protocol in the multicast address allocation architecture, used by a node, typically a router, to claim and allocate one or more address prefixes to that node's domain. Each prefix has an associated lifetime and is chosen out of a larger prefix with a lifetime at least as long, in a manner such that prefixes are aggregatable. At any time, each MASC node will typically advertise several prefixes with different lifetimes and scopes, which allows the Multicast Address Allocation Servers, or MAASs, in that domain or in child MASC domains to choose appropriate addresses for their clients.

The set of prefixes associated with a domain, the address set, is injected into an inter-domain routing protocol such as BGP4+, where an inter-domain multicast tree construction protocol can use it to build inter-domain group-shared trees.

The memo is careful about what claiming does and does not achieve. A domain does not need an address set for the hosts in it to be able to allocate group addresses, and allocating does not guarantee that hosts in other domains will not use an address in the set, since hosts are not forced to contact a MAAS before using a group address. Allocating an address set does ensure that inter-domain group-specific multicast distribution trees for any group in the set will be locally rooted, and that traffic will be sent outside the domain only when and where external receivers exist.

The key design requirements for the allocation mechanism are efficient address space utilization when space is scarce, which implies that allocation be based on actual usage patterns and therefore be dynamic; address aggregation, which implies that the mechanism be hierarchical; minimizing flux in the allocated address sets, so that address sets are reused when possible; and robustness, by using decentralized mechanisms. The timeliness of obtaining an address set is not a major design constraint, because that is handled at a lower level.
sections.plainLanguage: MASC gives a network its own block of multicast addresses so that the traffic for a group stays inside the network unless somebody outside actually wants it. The design goals are to use addresses efficiently, to group them so that routing tables stay small, and to avoid handing the same address to two networks.

sections.title: The Claim-Collide Mechanism
sections.content:
Typically one or more border routers of each domain that needs multicast address space run MASC. A MASC node, on behalf of its domain, chooses an address set to claim, sends a claim to other MASC domains in the network, and waits while listening for any colliding claims. If there is a collision, the losing claimer gives up the colliding claim and claims a different address set. After a sufficiently long collision-free waiting period, the address set chosen by the MASC node is considered allocated to that node's domain.

Three things may then happen. The allocated prefix can be injected as a multicast route into the inter-domain routing protocol as G-RIB Network Layer Reachability Information, where it may be used to construct group-shared trees, and MASC nodes may perform CIDR-like aggregation of the multicast information to keep the G-RIB small. The node's domain may assign to itself a sub-prefix for use by the MAASs within it. And sub-prefixes may be allocated to child domains.

The RFC explains why it chose a claim-collide mechanism rather than a query-response one. In a query-response mechanism, replicas of the MASC node would be needed in parent MASC domains so that their answers would survive failures, which brings the problem of keeping the replicas synchronized and possibly fragmenting the address space further. Even then, address collisions would still have to be handled. The authors believe the claim-collide mechanism is simpler and more robust.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of asking who owns an address, a node announces that it wants one and waits. If two nodes want the same address, one of them backs off and tries another. The waiting period is what makes this safe.

sections.title: The MASC Topology and the Life of a Prefix
sections.content:
The domain hierarchy used by MASC is congruent with the hierarchical structure of the inter-domain topology, for example backbones connected to regionals and regionals to metropolitan providers. As in BGP, MASC connections are locally configured. A MASC domain that is a customer of other MASC domains has one or more of those provider domains as its parent, and at the top a number of Top-Level Domains are connected in a sparse mesh and share the global multicast address space. To improve robustness, a pair of children of the same parent may be configured as siblings with regard to that parent.

All MASC communications use TCP. With respect to each remote node, the local node acts in one of four roles. As an INTERNAL_PEER, the two nodes are in the same MASC domain. As a CHILD, a customer relationship exists and the local node may obtain address space from the remote node. As a PARENT, the reverse holds. As a SIBLING, no customer and provider relationship exists. A node's message is propagated to its parent, all siblings with the same parent, and its children.

Each domain has a Managed Address Set, which is all the space the domain has successfully claimed via MASC, and a Locally-Allocated Address Set, which is the space MAASs inside the domain may use. The locally-allocated set is a subset of the managed set. For leaf domains, which have no children, the two sets are identical, since all claimed space is allocated for local use. A parent domain manages all the space it has claimed, while sub-prefixes can be allocated to itself and to its children.

Each prefix has an associated lifetime. A domain that wants to use a prefix longer than its lifetime must renew the prefix before the lifetime expires, and if the lifetime cannot be extended it should either retry later or choose and claim another prefix. After a prefix's lifetime expires, the MASC nodes in the domain that own it must stop using it, the entry must be removed from the G-RIB, and the information associated with it may be deleted from the node's local memory. Each prefix advertised by a parent to its children can be active or deprecated, and a deprecated prefix is one the parent wishes to discontinue after its lifetime expires; only active prefixes are candidates for size expansion or lifetime extension.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks form a tree, like the Internet itself, and a MASC node treats its neighbour as a parent, a child, a sibling or a partner in the same network. Every block of addresses has an expiry date, and a network that wants to keep using it has to renew it in time.

sections.title: Claiming, Renewing and Releasing Space
sections.content:
When a MASC node needs more address space, it decides locally the size and value of the address prefixes it will claim from one of its parents, based on what it knows about its parent's address set, its siblings' claims and allocations, its own address set, and the demand pattern of its children. A node that is not in a top-level domain can initiate a claim toward a parent only if it has an established connection with at least one node in that parent domain.

The claim then proceeds in four steps. The claim is scheduled to be sent after a random delay in the interval (0, [INITIATE_CLAIM_DELAY]), and if a claim from another node in the same domain arrives and removes the need for the local claim, the local claim is cancelled. The claim is sent to one of the parents, to all known siblings with the same parent, and to all internal peers, a Claim-Timer is started at [WAITING_PERIOD], and the node listens for colliding claims. If a colliding claim arrives while the timer runs, the two claims are compared, and if the local claim loses, a new prefix must be chosen and the losing claim's timer cancelled, either by explicitly withdrawing it or by letting it expire; if the winning claim came from a node in the same domain, no new claim is started. If the Claim-Timer expires, the claimed prefix becomes associated with the claimer's domain: the node advertises it to its parent and siblings with a PREFIX_IN_USE claim, injects it into the G-RIB, and sends a PREFIX_MANAGED message to all children and internal peers so that they may claim within the managed space.

The comparison of two claims uses the claim type first, with the precedence PREFIX_IN_USE over CLAIM_DENIED over CLAIM_TO_EXPAND over NEW_CLAIM. If the types are the same, the claim with the earliest timestamp wins, and if the timestamps are equal, the claim with the smallest origin node identifier wins.

Renewing a prefix uses the same procedure with the claim type CLAIM_TO_EXPAND and the same address and mask as the prefix already allocated. Expanding a prefix uses the same procedure with the claim type CLAIM_TO_EXPAND and the address and mask set to the desired larger values. Releasing space deletes the resources associated with the prefix, and, if the lifetime has not expired and no subranges have been allocated for local use or to children, the space may be released by sending a withdraw message to the parent, the siblings and the internal peers.
sections.plainLanguage: A claim waits a short random time before going out, so that two nodes in the same network do not both claim. The claim is then announced, and the sender waits for the full waiting period. If a competing claim turns up, the two are compared and one of them gives up.

sections.title: Message Formats and Constants
sections.content:
Messages are sent over a reliable transport protocol connection, a message is processed only after it is entirely received, and the maximum message size is 4096 octets, which all implementations must support. Each message has a fixed-size 4-octet header, with a data portion after it that may or may not be present. The Length field is a 2-octet unsigned integer giving the total length of the message including the header, which must always be at least 4 and no greater than 4096, and no padding of extra data is allowed. The Type field is a 1-octet unsigned integer with four defined codes: 1 for OPEN, 2 for UPDATE, 3 for NOTIFICATION and 4 for KEEPALIVE. The last octet is reserved, and must be set to zero by the sender and ignored by the receiver.

The first message sent by each side after a connection is established is an OPEN message, and if it is acceptable a KEEPALIVE message confirming the OPEN is sent back. After that, UPDATE, KEEPALIVE and NOTIFICATION messages may be exchanged. The minimum length of an OPEN message is 20 octets, and it carries a version number, currently 1, a 5-bit address family number, a 2-bit role field with the values 00 for INTERNAL_PEER, 01 for CHILD, 10 for SIBLING and 11 for PARENT, a 2-octet hold time, and three variable-length identifiers for the sender's domain, the sender's MASC node and the sender's parent domain.

UPDATE messages transfer claim, collision and prefix-managed information, and the minimum length of an UPDATE message is 40 octets. Each attribute has a length, a type and data, and all attributes are 4-octets aligned. The attribute types are 0 for PREFIX_IN_USE, 1 for CLAIM_DENIED, 2 for CLAIM_TO_EXPAND, 3 for NEW_CLAIM, 4 for PREFIX_MANAGED and 5 for WITHDRAW, with types 128 to 255 reserved for optional attributes.

The constants are the TCP port number 2587, the waiting period of 172800 seconds, or 48 hours, the random claim delay of 600 seconds, or 10 minutes, the hold time of 240 seconds, or 4 minutes, and the top-level domain identifier 0.
sections.plainLanguage: Every MASC message starts with four bytes that say how long it is and what kind it is. There are four kinds of message, and the UPDATE kind carries the claims themselves, each claim tagged with its type.

sections.title: The Connection State Machine
sections.content:
MASC operation is specified in terms of a finite state machine for the peering session, which starts in the Idle state, where MASC refuses all incoming connections from the peer and allocates no resources to the remote node. The Start event, generated by either system or operator, initializes the MASC resources, starts the ConnectRetry timer, initiates a transport connection to the remote node while listening for one that the remote node may initiate, and moves to the Connect state. Getting out of Idle requires a Start event, and to avoid persistent flapping when a node keeps returning to Idle after an error, the time between automatically generated Start events should increase exponentially, starting at 60 seconds, doubling on each retry, and not exceeding 24 hours.

In the Connect state MASC waits for the transport connection to be completed. If it succeeds, the ConnectRetry timer is cleared, an OPEN message is sent and the state becomes OpenSent. If it fails, the ConnectRetry timer restarts and the state becomes Active, where MASC waits for the remote node to initiate the connection.

In the OpenSent state MASC waits for an OPEN message and checks all its fields. If an error is found or a connection collision is detected, a NOTIFICATION message is sent and, if the connection is to be closed, the state becomes Idle. If there are no errors, MASC sends a KEEPALIVE message, replaces the provisional hold timer with the negotiated hold time, and moves to OpenConfirm. In the OpenConfirm state MASC waits for a KEEPALIVE or NOTIFICATION message, and a KEEPALIVE moves it to the Established state, where UPDATE, NOTIFICATION and KEEPALIVE messages can be exchanged. A NOTIFICATION with the O-bit zeroed, an expired hold timer, or a Stop event moves the session back to Idle, and the MASC connection is closed and its resources released.
sections.plainLanguage: Each MASC session moves through a fixed set of states: idle, trying to connect, waiting for the peer's OPEN, confirming the OPEN, and then established. An error at any point sends the session back to idle, where an operator has to start it again.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Total length of the message including the header, in octets; at least 4 and no greater than 4096.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Message type: 1 OPEN, 2 UPDATE, 3 NOTIFICATION, 4 KEEPALIVE.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to zero by the sender and ignored by the receiver.

viz.caption: THE CLAIM TYPES CARRIED IN AN UPDATE ATTRIBUTE

items.label: PREFIX_IN_USE
items.desc: The prefix is being used by the origin.

items.label: CLAIM_DENIED
items.desc: The claim is refused, probably by the origin's parent domain.

items.label: CLAIM_TO_EXPAND
items.desc: The origin is trying to expand the size of an existing prefix.

items.label: NEW_CLAIM
items.desc: The origin is trying to claim a new prefix.

items.label: PREFIX_MANAGED
items.desc: The parent is informing a child that space is available.

items.label: WITHDRAW
items.desc: The origin is withdrawing a previous claim.
